questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the independent variable in an experiment
questions.stem: A researcher tests whether sleep duration affects reaction time by assigning participants to sleep 4, 6, or 8 hours. What is the independent variable?

options.misconception: confuses the measured outcome with the manipulated factor
confuses the subjects with the variable
confuses a design feature with the variable being tested

questions.explanation: The independent variable is the factor the researcher manipulates, which is sleep duration. Reaction time is the dependent variable because it is measured, the participants are the subjects, and the number of groups is a design choice, so each distractor names a real feature of the study applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: Which factor is manipulated?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: identify the dependent variable in an experiment
questions.stem: A researcher measures heart rate after assigning participants to caffeine or decaf. What is the dependent variable?

options.misconception: confuses the manipulated factor with the measured outcome
confuses sample size with the measured outcome
confuses a procedure with the measured outcome

questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the outcome the researcher measures, which is heart rate. Caffeine condition is manipulated, the number of participants is a sample feature, and random assignment is a procedure, so each distractor names a real study feature applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: Which outcome is measured?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose of a control group
questions.stem: In a drug trial, one group receives the active drug and another receives an inert pill. What is the main purpose of the inert-pill group?

options.text: It directly tests the placebo effect
options.misconception: confuses a possible side observation with the main comparison purpose

options.text: It removes the need for randomization
options.misconception: confuses a control group with random assignment
confuses a control group with blinding

questions.explanation: The control group provides a comparison baseline so researchers can judge whether the treatment has an effect beyond the control condition. Testing placebo effects, randomization, and blinding are separate design issues, so each distractor names a real study feature applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: Why include a group that does not receive the active treatment?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain why random assignment reduces bias
questions.stem: Participants are randomly assigned to treatment conditions. What problem does this procedure primarily reduce?

options.text: It reduces selection bias by balancing pre-existing differences
It ensures every population member can be sampled
options.misconception: confuses random assignment with random sampling

options.text: It makes the sample representative of the population
options.misconception: confuses assignment with sampling representativeness

options.text: It eliminates measurement error in the dependent variable
options.misconception: confuses group assignment with measurement accuracy

questions.explanation: Random assignment distributes pre-existing differences across groups, reducing selection bias and strengthening causal inference. It does not by itself create a representative sample or fix measurement error, so each distractor names a real research goal applied to the wrong procedure.
questions.hint: What kind of bias comes from pre-existing group differences?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A psychologist defines aggression as the number of pushes during a 10-minute observation. This is an example of what?

options.misconception: confuses a measurement rule with a prediction
confuses a measurement rule with an extraneous factor
confuses a measurement rule with a population value

questions.explanation: An operational definition specifies exactly how a concept is measured, here by counting pushes. A hypothesis makes a prediction, a confound is an extraneous influence, and a population parameter describes a whole population, so each distractor names a real research term applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: Which term describes how a concept is measured?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In a study of study time and exam scores, students who study more also sleep less. Sleep is best described as what?

options.misconception: confuses an extraneous factor with the manipulated factor
confuses an extraneous factor with the measured outcome
confuses an extraneous factor with a comparison group

questions.explanation: Sleep is a confounding variable because it is related to both study time and exam performance and can distort the apparent relationship. It is not the manipulated factor, the measured outcome, or a comparison group, so each distractor names a real study feature applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: What factor could distort the relationship between study time and scores?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Participants improve after receiving a sugar pill they believe is medicine. This outcome best illustrates what?

options.misconception: confuses treatment-expectation effects with being observed
confuses participant expectations about the study with placebo response
confuses natural score fluctuation with treatment expectation

questions.explanation: The placebo effect occurs when improvement follows an inert treatment because of expectations. The Hawthorne effect involves changed behavior due to observation, demand characteristics involve cues about desired responses, and regression to the mean involves extreme scores moving toward average, so each distractor names a real phenomenon applied to the wrong cause.
questions.hint: What happens when an inert treatment produces improvement?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In a clinical trial, neither participants nor researchers know who receives the treatment. This design is called what?

options.misconception: confuses partial blinding with full blinding
confuses no blinding with full blinding
confuses use of a placebo with blinding of roles

questions.explanation: A double-blind design keeps both participants and researchers unaware of condition assignment, reducing bias. Single-blind blinds only one group, open-label blinds no one, and placebo-controlled refers to using a placebo rather than to who is blinded, so each distractor names a real design feature applied to the wrong concept.
questions.hint: Who is kept unaware of condition assignment?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A statement predicting that more sleep leads to better memory performance is best described as what?

options.misconception: confuses a predicted effect with a no-effect statement
confuses a prediction with a measurement rule
confuses a prediction with the list of population members

questions.explanation: A directional hypothesis predicts the direction of an effect, such as more sleep improving memory. The null hypothesis states no effect, an operational definition specifies measurement, and a sampling frame lists possible participants, so each distractor names a real research term applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: Does the statement predict a direction of effect?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The null hypothesis in an experiment states that...

options.text: There is no effect or difference between conditions

options.misconception: confuses the null hypothesis with the alternative hypothesis
confuses the null hypothesis with a sampling assumption
confuses the null hypothesis with measurement quality

questions.explanation: The null hypothesis states there is no effect or difference between conditions. The alternative predicts an effect, representativeness concerns sampling, and reliability concerns measurement consistency, so each distractor names a real research concept applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: What would be expected if the treatment has no effect?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A p-value of .03 is best interpreted as what?

options.text: The probability of the observed result if the null hypothesis is true
The probability that the hypothesis is true
options.misconception: confuses a p-value with posterior probability

options.text: The size of the effect in the sample
options.misconception: confuses a p-value with effect size
confuses a p-value with measurement reliability

questions.explanation: A p-value gives the probability of observing the data, or more extreme data, if the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that a hypothesis is true, the effect size, or reliability, so each distractor names a real statistical concept applied to the wrong interpretation.
questions.hint: What is assumed true when computing the p-value?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is called what?

options.misconception: confuses a false positive with a false negative
confuses rejecting a true null with failing to reject a false null
confuses a hypothesis-testing error with sampling variability

questions.explanation: A Type I error is a false positive: rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true. A Type II error is the opposite, a false negative is failing to detect a true effect, and sampling error is chance variation in sampling, so each distractor names a real error concept applied to the wrong case.
questions.hint: What is the false-positive error called?

provenance.author: bank-team-p3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is called what?

options.misconception: confuses a false negative with a false positive
confuses failing to detect an effect with detecting a nonexistent one
confuses a hypothesis-testing error with measurement inaccuracy

questions.explanation: A Type II error is a false negative: failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false. A Type I error is the opposite, a false positive is detecting a nonexistent effect, and measurement error concerns instrument inaccuracy, so each distractor names a real error concept applied to the wrong case.
questions.hint: What is the false-negative error called?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A conventional alpha level of .05 means what?

options.text: The maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error
The probability of a Type II error
options.misconception: confuses alpha with beta
confuses a significance threshold with effect magnitude
confuses alpha with sample-size planning

questions.explanation: Alpha sets the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error before the null hypothesis is rejected. Beta concerns Type II error, effect size concerns magnitude, and sample size is a separate planning issue, so each distractor names a real statistical concept applied to the wrong role.
questions.hint: What error probability does alpha control?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A strong positive correlation between ice cream sales and drowning rates does not imply what?

options.text: That ice cream consumption causes drowning

options.misconception: confuses absence of causation with absence of relationship
confuses causation with covariation

options.text: That data on both variables were collected
options.misconception: confuses causation with data collection

questions.explanation: Correlation shows that variables covary, but it does not by itself establish causation. The distractors state things that can be true even when causation is not established, so each one confuses a weaker or unrelated claim with a causal claim.
questions.hint: What can correlation not establish?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A researcher surveys only students studying in the campus library. This sample most likely suffers from what?

options.misconception: confuses systematic selection bias with chance fluctuation
confuses participant selection with measurement inaccuracy
confuses selection bias with dropout over time

questions.explanation: Surveying only library users systematically excludes other students, creating sampling bias. Random error is chance variation, measurement error concerns instrument accuracy, and attrition concerns dropout, so each distractor names a real research issue applied to the wrong cause.
questions.hint: Does the selection method systematically exclude some students?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Every member of the population has an equal chance of selection. This procedure is called what?

options.misconception: confuses selecting participants with assigning conditions
confuses equal chance with subgroup-based sampling
confuses probability sampling with ease-based sampling

questions.explanation: Random sampling gives every population member an equal chance of being selected. Random assignment concerns condition allocation, stratified sampling uses subgroups, and convenience sampling selects easy-to-reach participants, so each distractor names a real sampling or design term applied to the wrong procedure.
questions.hint: Is the procedure about selecting participants or assigning conditions?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The population is divided into subgroups, and samples are drawn from each subgroup. This is what?

options.misconception: confuses subgroup sampling with sampling whole clusters
confuses subgroup sampling with fixed-interval selection
confuses probability stratification with nonprobability quotas

questions.explanation: Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups and samples from each. Cluster sampling selects whole clusters, systematic sampling selects at fixed intervals, and quota sampling uses nonprobability quotas, so each distractor names a real sampling method applied to the wrong procedure.
questions.hint: Are participants sampled from every subgroup?

provenance.author: bank-team-p3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Selecting participants because they are easy to reach is called what?

options.misconception: confuses nonprobability ease with probability methods
confuses ease-based selection with equal-chance selection
confuses ease-based selection with subgroup sampling

questions.explanation: Convenience sampling selects participants based on ease of access. Probability sampling uses random selection, random sampling gives equal chance, and stratified sampling uses subgroups, so each distractor names a real sampling method applied to the wrong procedure.
questions.hint: Is selection based on ease of access?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Different participants are assigned to each experimental condition. This is a what?

options.misconception: confuses different participants with same participants across conditions
confuses independent groups with paired matching
confuses group comparison with one participant

questions.explanation: A between-subjects design assigns different participants to each condition. Within-subjects uses the same participants, matched-pairs pairs similar participants, and single-case focuses on one participant, so each distractor names a real design applied to the wrong structure.
questions.hint: Are different people in each condition?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The same participants experience all experimental conditions. This is a what?

options.misconception: confuses same participants with different participants across conditions
confuses repeated measures with separate groups
confuses repeated measures with blocking

questions.explanation: A within-subjects design exposes the same participants to all conditions. Between-subjects uses different participants, independent-groups also separates participants, and randomized-block groups similar participants, so each distractor names a real design applied to the wrong structure.
questions.hint: Do the same people experience every condition?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: In a within-subjects study, the order of conditions is varied across participants to reduce what?

options.misconception: confuses sequence effects with participant selection bias
confuses sequence effects with treatment expectations
confuses sequence effects with instrument inaccuracy

questions.explanation: Counterbalancing varies condition order to reduce order effects such as practice or fatigue. Sampling bias concerns participant selection, placebo effects concern expectations, and measurement error concerns instrument accuracy, so each distractor names a real research issue applied to the wrong problem.
questions.hint: What problem comes from experiencing conditions in a fixed order?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The degree to which a study establishes a causal relationship is called what?

options.misconception: confuses causal inference with generalizability
confuses causal inference with measuring the intended concept
confuses causal inference with statistical conclusion accuracy

questions.explanation: Internal validity is the degree to which a study supports a causal conclusion. External validity concerns generalizability, construct validity concerns whether the intended concept is measured, and statistical validity concerns the accuracy of statistical conclusions, so each distractor names a real validity type applied to the wrong question.
questions.hint: Which validity type concerns causal conclusions?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: The extent to which results generalize to other settings or populations is called what?

options.misconception: confuses generalizability with causal inference
confuses generalizability with surface plausibility
confuses generalizability with coverage of a domain

questions.explanation: External validity concerns generalizing results to other settings, populations, or times. Internal validity concerns causal inference, face validity concerns surface plausibility, and content validity concerns coverage of a content domain, so each distractor names a real validity type applied to the wrong question.
questions.hint: Which validity type concerns generalizing results?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A measure gives consistent results across repeated administrations. This property is called what?

options.misconception: confuses consistency with measuring the intended construct
confuses consistency with applying results broadly
confuses consistency with likelihood under the null hypothesis

questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency of measurement across repeated administrations. Validity concerns measuring the intended construct, generalizability concerns applying results broadly, and statistical significance concerns likelihood under the null hypothesis, so each distractor names a real research concept applied to the wrong property.
questions.hint: Which property concerns consistency?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A test measures what it claims to measure. This property is called what?

options.misconception: confuses the intended construct with consistency
confuses the intended construct with ability to detect effects
confuses the intended construct with sample economy

questions.explanation: Validity is whether a test measures what it claims to measure. Reliability concerns consistency, statistical power concerns detecting effects, and sampling efficiency concerns sample economy, so each distractor names a real research concept applied to the wrong property.
questions.hint: Which property concerns measuring the intended construct?

provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Repeating a study to determine whether findings hold is called what?

options.misconception: confuses repeating a study with assigning conditions randomly
confuses repeating a study with varying condition order
confuses repeating a study with subgroup sampling

questions.explanation: Replication repeats a study to see whether findings hold. Randomization assigns conditions, counterbalancing varies order, and stratification samples subgroups, so each distractor names a real research procedure applied to the wrong purpose.
questions.hint: Which term means repeating a study?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: A statistic that indicates the magnitude of a difference or relationship is called what?

options.misconception: confuses magnitude with probability under the null hypothesis
confuses magnitude with a range of plausible values
confuses magnitude with sampling variability

questions.explanation: Effect size indicates the magnitude of a difference or relationship. A p-value concerns probability under the null hypothesis, a confidence interval gives a range of plausible values, and a standard error concerns sampling variability, so each distractor names a real statistical concept applied to the wrong quantity.
questions.hint: Which statistic measures magnitude?

provenance.author: bank-team-p3
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.stem: Results are statistically significant when they are...

options.misconception: confuses statistical significance with practical importance
confuses significance with replicability
confuses significance with absence of sampling variability

questions.explanation: Statistical significance means the observed result is unlikely under the null hypothesis at the chosen alpha level. Practical importance is effect size, replicability is not guaranteed by significance, and sampling error is never fully absent, so each distractor names a real research concept applied to the wrong interpretation.
questions.hint: What does significance say about the null hypothesis?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: compute the standard error of the mean
questions.stem: A sample has standard deviation 12 and size 36. What is the standard error of the mean?
questions.explanation: Standard error equals standard deviation divided by the square root of sample size: 12 / sqrt(36) = 2.
questions.hint: Divide the standard deviation by the square root of n.
